ut.title: Ultrasonic Testing & UT Thickness Inspection | Charlotte, NC
ut.description: On-site ultrasonic thickness testing and weld UT for Charlotte-area power plants, fabricators and process sites, with Level III review. Request a quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) and Thickness Inspection in Charlotte, North Carolina
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT sends ultrasonic technicians to Charlotte-area power plants, fabrication shops, process facilities and construction sites for thickness surveys and weld examination on carbon and low-alloy steel. Typical jobs are steam and feedwater piping grids, boiler and vessel wall thickness, plate checks before cutting, and shear-wave examination of structural and pressure welds. Request a UT quote for your Charlotte site with drawings, line lists and the governing code, and we reply within one business day.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in Charlotte

Charlotte sits at the center of a power-industry region. Utility fleets across the Carolinas run steam-cycle plants, combined-cycle units and nuclear stations, and the engineering and supply chain around them is concentrated here. Siemens Energy builds gas turbines in the city, which pulls heavy plate, forgings and welded casings through local fabrication and machining shops. All of that steel eventually needs a wall thickness number or a weld examination, and ultrasonic testing is the method that provides both from one side of the component.

Three kinds of work dominate in this market:

  • Power and process plants: feedwater, condensate and extraction steam piping, heater drain lines, boiler tubes and headers, deaerators, and pressure vessels.
  • Fabrication and manufacturing: plate lamination checks before cutting, shear-wave examination of production welds on vessels and structural assemblies, and thickness checks on machined stock.
  • Construction: Charlotte's downtown and corridor development uses a large amount of structural steel, and groove welds in heavy connections can be specified for ultrasonic examination under the structural welding code.

Warehouse and distribution buildings, rail terminals and the airport district also add storage tanks, air receivers and structural members that are thickness-checked on a maintenance cycle.

What UT finds, and what it misses

Ultrasonic testing sends sound into the material and listens for reflections. A reflection from the back wall gives thickness; a reflection from somewhere in between signals a discontinuity such as a lamination, a crack, lack of fusion or slag. Because sound travels through the full wall, UT reports the remaining thickness of a corroded pipe or vessel directly, and it finds planar flaws buried in a weld that surface methods never see.

Limits matter as much as strengths. Sound needs a smooth enough surface and couplant to get in, so heavy scale, flaking paint or deep pitting scatter the signal and must be dressed first. Coarse-grained castings and some austenitic welds attenuate the beam. Very thin wall, under a few tenths of an inch, can double the echo and give a false reading if the display is not read carefully. Flaws that sit parallel to the beam, or very close to the surface in the dead zone, can be missed by a single probe. A procedure written for the specific material and geometry is how those limits are managed rather than ignored.

How a thickness survey is carried out

Thickness work in Charlotte plants follows the same logic as an API 570 or API 510 program: a set of condition monitoring locations is marked on each line or vessel, and the same points are read at every campaign so the corrosion rate is a measured number. The technician calibrates the gauge on a step block of the same material, using a dual-element probe where the outside surface is rough or the inside is pitted. The display is read as an A-scan, not only as a digital number, so a doubled echo or a lamination is recognized rather than reported as thickness.

On hot service lines the work needs a high-temperature probe and couplant, and the velocity correction for temperature is applied or the gauge is calibrated on a block at a similar temperature. For flow-accelerated corrosion, a fixed grid is marked at elbows, tees, reducers and downstream of control valves, and the grid is read to the same layout each outage so the wear pattern becomes visible. Readings are tied to a component identifier, never to a loose list of numbers.

Weld examination with angle beams

For welds, the technician uses angle-beam shear-wave probes, usually 45, 60 and 70 degrees, chosen to meet the weld bevel at a useful angle. A reference level or distance-amplitude curve is built from side-drilled holes in a calibration block, the scan covers the weld and heat-affected zone from both sides where access allows, and each indication is located, sized by length and amplitude, and compared with the acceptance criteria of the construction code.

UT is strong at lack of fusion, cracks and slag in thicker welds, which is why codes such as ASME Section VIII Division 1 and AWS D1.1 allow it, and why ASME B31.3 and API 1104 contain ultrasonic provisions. It does not give a picture the way film does, so the report relies on a written scan plan, sketches and recorded amplitudes. Where an owner wants a permanent image of a weld, that is a decision for the engineer and the code, not something this page can settle.

Codes and acceptance criteria for Charlotte work

The examination method comes from ASME Section V: Article 4 for weld examination, Article 5 for materials and Article 23 for contact thickness measurement under SE-797. The acceptance criteria come from the document that governs the item. Boilers and power piping run to ASME Section I and B31.1, process piping to ASME B31.3, vessels to Section VIII, structural steel to AWS D1.1 (with the examination provisions in Clause 8 of the 2020 edition), and in-service equipment to API 510, API 570 or API 653. Under those API codes the owner's authorized inspector is responsible for the inspection; Atlantis performs the ultrasonic work and reports the data, such as thickness at each condition monitoring location.

ASTM E797 covers contact pulse-echo thickness measurement, E164 covers contact examination of weldments, and E114 covers straight-beam work. Which edition applies is set by the contract, so the first step on any Charlotte job is to confirm the code year the owner is working to.

North Carolina rules that touch UT work

Boilers and pressure vessels in North Carolina fall under the Uniform Boiler and Pressure Vessel Act, administered by the Boiler Safety Bureau of the state Department of Labor. Equipment must carry a current inspection certificate, intervals depend on the type of equipment, and welded repairs and alterations follow the National Board Inspection Code, with a National Board R-stamped repair organization. Ultrasonic data supports those inspections and repair records but does not replace the inspector's role.

North Carolina also operates its own occupational safety and health plan, so site orientation, fall protection on boiler scaffolds and confined-space entry follow state enforcement. At chemical facilities covered by OSHA process safety management, 29 CFR 1910.119(j) asks that mechanical integrity inspections follow recognized and generally accepted good engineering practice, which in practice means the API and ASME documents above. Nuclear station work runs under its own quality and personnel-qualification programs and is outside the scope of this page.

Who performs the examination

Atlantis technicians are qualified under the company's written practice, which is built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. On a Charlotte job, the Level II technician calibrates the instrument, scans the component and judges what the display shows. An ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews reports, and the employer, not an outside body, issues the qualification under that written practice. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. If your site requires qualification to a different standard, that should be named at the quoting stage so the scope can be matched or declined honestly.

What the UT report contains

A usable report carries the component identifier and drawing reference, the procedure number and revision, the instrument, probe and calibration block used, the calibration check record, and the name and level of the technician. For thickness work it adds a grid or CML table with each reading, the nominal and minimum required thickness, and any location where wall is below the retirement value. For weld work it adds the scan plan, the reference level, each reportable indication with location, length and amplitude, and an accept or reject decision against the named criteria. Sketches and photographs of the marked component are attached so the next campaign can find the same points.

Planning a UT job in Charlotte

Technicians travel to your site, so planning is mostly about access and conditions. Charlotte summers are hot and humid, and steel exposed to sun can run well above ambient, which affects couplant behavior and probe wear. Winters are milder than in the Midwest, but a cold morning on an uninsulated line still changes couplant viscosity. Utility outages are scheduled in the spring and fall shoulder seasons, and fabrication shops run on their own delivery calendars, so dates need to be agreed early. Plant badging, safety orientation and scaffolding should be arranged before the crew mobilizes, and a short list of drawings, isometrics and line numbers speeds the quote. We do not keep an office in Charlotte, and the quote reflects travel to your site.

UT, MT or PT for your Charlotte job

Choose ultrasonic testing when you need wall thickness or volumetric information about a weld. Choose magnetic particle inspection in Charlotte when the question is surface or near-surface cracking in carbon or low-alloy steel, such as toe cracks, crane hooks or attachment welds. Choose liquid penetrant testing in Charlotte for stainless steel, nickel alloys and aluminum, or any surface-breaking flaw on non-magnetic material. Many jobs combine them: UT for thickness and root condition, MT or PT on the repair weld. The national pages on ultrasonic testing and the ultrasonic testing guide explain the method in more depth.

Training your own UT technicians

If your plant would rather qualify its own people, Atlantis teaches UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training, and trainees can practice scanning on the UT practical simulator. Local details for the area are on the Charlotte NDT training page. Under SNT-TC-1A your company certifies its own employees through its written practice; the training supports that process and does not replace it.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in Charlotte for ultrasonic testing?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Charlotte. Technicians are mobilized to your plant, shop or construction site for the agreed scope, working under a written practice built on SNT-TC-1A with an ASNT Level III approving procedures.

faq.q: What is ultrasonic thickness testing used for at Charlotte power plants?
faq.a: It measures remaining wall on boiler tubes, headers, feedwater and condensate piping, and vessels. Readings are taken at fixed locations so the corrosion rate can be tracked from one outage to the next.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing replace radiography on a weld?
faq.a: Sometimes. ASME Section VIII, B31.3, API 1104 and AWS D1.1 each contain ultrasonic provisions, but substitution has conditions and must be agreed with the owner, the engineer and the authorized inspector before work starts.

faq.q: What surface preparation does UT need?
faq.a: The scan surface must be free of loose scale, flaking coating and weld spatter so the probe couples cleanly. Light wire brushing is often enough for thickness; weld scanning may need the cap ground flat, and the procedure states what is required.

faq.q: Which standards govern UT weld inspection in the Charlotte area?
faq.a: The method is set by ASME Section V Article 4, and acceptance by the construction code, such as ASME Section VIII, B31.3, API 1104 or AWS D1.1 for structural steel. Your contract names the edition.

faq.q: How are hot piping lines examined?
faq.a: The technician uses a high-temperature probe and couplant, applies a velocity correction or calibrates on a block at a similar temperature, and limits contact time. Very hot lines may need to be cooled or examined during an outage.

faq.q: Does Atlantis inspect nuclear station equipment around Charlotte?
faq.a: No. Nuclear in-service inspection has its own quality program and personnel qualification requirements. Atlantis ultrasonic work in this area is on conventional boilers, piping, vessels, tanks, fabrication and structural steel.

faq.q: What do I need to send to get a UT quote for Charlotte?
faq.a: Send drawings or isometrics, line or vessel numbers, material and wall thickness, the code and edition, access conditions, and target dates. If condition monitoring locations already exist, include the list.

faq.q: Can my own technicians learn ultrasonic testing through Atlantis?
faq.a: Yes. Atlantis offers UT Level 1 and Level 2 training and a practical simulator. Your company then qualifies and certifies its technicians under its own written practice, as SNT-TC-1A requires.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MPI) in Charlotte, NC | MT
mt.description: On-site magnetic particle inspection and mag particle testing for Charlotte-area power plants, fabricators and lifting equipment. Ask for an MT quote today.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Charlotte, North Carolina
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes magnetic particle inspectors to Charlotte-area plants, fabrication shops, rail facilities and construction sites to find surface and near-surface cracks in carbon and low-alloy steel. Common work includes boiler and header attachment welds, structural connections, crane hooks and lifting lugs, shafts and race-shop steel parts. Ask for an MT quote for your Charlotte job, listing the parts, material and code, and we answer within one business day.

Where magnetic particle inspection is used in Charlotte

The industrial mix around Charlotte gives MPI a steady list of targets. Utility plants have welded attachments on boiler headers, stub tubes and supports where fatigue cracking begins at the toe of a weld. Fabrication shops serving the energy equipment supply chain weld thick carbon steel casings, bases and frames that are checked during fit-up and after final welding. Steel erection on the city's towers and corridor projects produces moment connections and column splices that are examined at the welds. Hooks, shackles, sheave blocks and lugs on shop cranes and mobile cranes are checked for cracks on periodic inspection.

Northeast of the city, around Concord and Mooresville, motorsport teams build steel chassis and suspension parts, and those ferromagnetic components are a natural fit for mag particle testing. Freight rail operations in the region add couplers, truck components and structural steel on rolling stock repair.

  • Power plant welds: header and stub attachments, support lugs, casing seams
  • Fabrication: in-process checks on fit-up, tack and root repairs, and completed pressure and structural welds
  • Lifting equipment: hooks, lugs, shackles, pins, crane runway attachments
  • Rotating and rolling parts: shafts, couplings, wheels and axle parts brought to the equipment

What MT finds, and what it cannot

Magnetic particle testing works on ferromagnetic material only. Carbon steel, low-alloy steel and martensitic stainless grades respond; austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, copper and titanium do not. The part is magnetized, fine iron particles are applied, and a crack that interrupts the magnetic field draws the particles into a visible line. The method finds surface-breaking cracks and, in suitable conditions, discontinuities a short distance below the surface, such as lack of fusion at a weld toe.

It will not size depth, it does not see deep internal flaws, and thick coatings reduce sensitivity because they hold the particles away from the field leakage. A crack that runs along the field lines produces little leakage, which is why each area is examined twice with the field turned about ninety degrees. Heavy scale, oil and weld spatter hide indications and are cleaned off first.

Choosing the technique

A good MT procedure states its choices. The magnetizing method is usually an electromagnetic yoke for field welds, with prods or cables on heavy sections and coils or a central conductor on parts that can be positioned. Alternating current concentrates flux at the surface and suits surface cracks, while direct or half-wave current reaches slightly deeper. Particles can be dry powder, which suits rough or warm surfaces, wet visible particles on a white contrast paint, or wet fluorescent particles viewed under UV-A light in a dark enclosure, which gives the highest sensitivity.

ASME Section V Article 7 sets the lifting-power check for yokes: at least 10 pounds for an AC yoke and at least 40 pounds for a DC or permanent-magnet yoke at the maximum pole spacing used. Field direction and strength are verified with a pie gauge or shim indicators, and the procedure records the choice.

Codes and acceptance criteria for Charlotte work

The method comes from ASME Section V Article 7 and ASTM E1444, with ASTM E709 as the guide. Acceptance comes from the construction or service code: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6 for vessels, ASME B31.3 for process piping with examination under paragraph 344.3, B31.1 for power piping, and AWS D1.1 for structural steel. For in-service equipment under API 510, API 570 or API 653, the owner's authorized inspector is responsible for the inspection and Atlantis performs the MT and reports the indications. The contract names the code year, and the first action on a job is to confirm it.

North Carolina requirements

The state Boiler Safety Bureau, part of the North Carolina Department of Labor, administers the Uniform Boiler and Pressure Vessel Act. Boilers and pressure vessels carry inspection certificates, and welded repairs follow the National Board Inspection Code with an R-stamped repair organization. MT on a repair weld becomes part of that repair record. Because North Carolina runs its own occupational safety and health plan, crane and hoist inspection programs, work at height and electrical safety around magnetizing equipment fall under state enforcement at plants in the Charlotte area.

Lifting equipment and the phrase magnet inspection

People searching for a magnet inspection service sometimes mean the periodic inspection of lifting magnets, which falls under ASME B30.20 and is carried out by the owner's designated person. That is not magnetic particle testing. MT enters lifting work when hooks, lugs, pins and crane structure must be checked for cracks, for example during the inspections ASME B30.10 requires for hooks. Atlantis performs the MT; it does not rate or approve the lifting device.

Surface preparation, coatings and weld condition

Magnetic particles need a clean, dry surface they can move across. Loose scale, grease, weld spatter and flaking paint are removed before the examination, and rough weld caps may need light grinding so indications are not confused with the weld profile. Thin non-magnetic coatings can stay in place if the procedure shows they do not hide the indications, and the technician demonstrates this with a known flaw or a shim indicator. Heavy coatings on steel structures, which are common in the Charlotte area where weather protection is applied soon after erection, usually have to be removed locally. Thick galvanizing and metallized layers also reduce sensitivity and are treated the same way.

Reading indications correctly

Not every line of particles is a crack. The technician separates relevant indications, which come from discontinuities, from non-relevant ones caused by magnetic writing, changes in section, sharp fillet corners or the edge of a weld. A suspected crack is re-examined after light surface conditioning, and if the line stays, it is recorded and measured. Indications are classed as linear when length exceeds three times width, and rounded otherwise, which is the distinction most acceptance tables use. Atlantis reports what was found and where, and leaves repair decisions to the owner and the inspector responsible under the code.

Weld toe cracking and thick carbon steel

Thick carbon steel welds that cool quickly or are made without enough preheat can develop hydrogen-assisted cracks hours or days after welding. Because of that, owners often specify that final MT on heavy sections be delayed until after the hold time in the welding procedure. If your scope includes crane runway beams, heavy base plates or thick header attachments, ask the fabricator for the delay period and place the inspection date accordingly, so the examination is meaningful and does not need to be repeated.

Field safety and equipment checks

Magnetizing equipment brings its own hazards. Yokes and prods draw current, so cables, plugs and ground-fault protection are checked before use, and prods are never energized away from the work surface because of arc burns. On a boiler scaffold or an elevated steel connection, the technician works under the site's fall-protection plan, and in confined spaces the atmosphere and ventilation come first. Before the job starts, the yoke is lift-tested with a calibrated weight, the UV light meter and white-light meter are within their calibration dates, and the particle suspension is checked for concentration with a settling test. Those records go in the report so an auditor can see the equipment was fit for the day.

Who does the work

MT is performed by Level II personnel qualified under the company's written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. Level II technicians set up the equipment, perform the examination and evaluate indications. An ASNT Level III writes or approves the procedure and reviews the reports, and Anoop Rayavarapu holds ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. The employer issues the qualification under SNT-TC-1A. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001.

What the MT report contains

The report names the component and its location on the drawing, the procedure and revision, the equipment and the yoke lifting-power check, the particle type, contrast paint or UV intensity, and the lighting level used. It records the surface condition and any cleaning, the technician and level, and each indication with position, length and orientation. Accept and reject decisions cite the code paragraph, and photographs of reportable indications are attached. If the procedure calls for demagnetization, the report states how residual field was checked afterward, because leftover magnetism can deflect a welding arc or attract chips into bearings.

Planning an MT job in Charlotte

Technicians travel to your site with portable equipment, so access, power and light are the planning issues. Dry powder and visible wet methods work outdoors in daylight; fluorescent work needs shade or a tent, and bright Carolina sun makes darkening harder in summer. Hot surfaces dry the carrier fluid quickly and degrade particles, so dry powder is often chosen for warm components. Power outage seasons fill up in spring and fall, and steel erection has its own sequence, so dates should be fixed early. Safety orientation and badging at plants take time. We have no office in Charlotte, and scope is quoted from your drawings.

MT, PT or UT for your Charlotte job

On carbon and low-alloy steel, MT is usually quicker and more sensitive than penetrant for tight cracks on rough welds. Move to dye penetrant inspection in Charlotte for stainless steel, aluminum or a joint where a yoke cannot seat. Use ultrasonic testing in Charlotte when depth or internal condition matters. For background, read the magnetic particle testing guide, the MT versus PT comparison and the national page on magnetic particle testing.

Training your own MT technicians

Plants that want in-house capability can start with MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training, with local details on the Charlotte NDT training page. Your company certifies its technicians under its own written practice, and the training supports that process.

faq.q: What is magnetic particle inspection used for in Charlotte?
faq.a: It finds surface and near-surface cracks in ferromagnetic steel: boiler header attachments, structural welds, crane hooks and lugs, shafts, and race-shop steel parts. It is used during fabrication, outages and periodic equipment checks.

faq.q: Can MT be done on stainless steel or aluminum?
faq.a: Not on austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, copper or titanium, because they are not ferromagnetic. For those materials, liquid penetrant testing is the surface method, and ultrasonic testing covers internal conditions.

faq.q: Does Atlantis keep an office or crew in Charlotte?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Charlotte. Qualified Level II technicians travel to your site with portable yokes and materials, and an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report.

faq.q: Should a Charlotte job use fluorescent particles or dry powder?
faq.a: Fluorescent particles under UV-A light give the highest sensitivity but need a darkened area. Dry powder works on rough or warm surfaces outdoors. The procedure states which is used and why.

faq.q: Why is the part examined twice?
faq.a: A crack shows best when it crosses the magnetic field. By examining each area twice with the field turned about ninety degrees, cracks in any orientation are detected, as ASME Section V Article 7 requires.

faq.q: Is demagnetization always required?
faq.a: No. It is required when residual magnetism could interfere with later welding, machining, bearing operation or instruments. The procedure states when it is needed and how the residual field will be checked.

faq.q: Is a magnet inspection service the same as MT?
faq.a: No. Inspection of lifting magnets falls under ASME B30.20 and belongs to the owner. MT is a crack-detection method that can be applied to hooks, lugs and crane structure.

faq.q: What do I send to request an MT quote for Charlotte?
faq.a: Send the part list or drawings, material, coating condition, applicable code and edition, access and power availability, and target dates. Photographs of the weld areas help the procedure choice.

faq.q: Can Atlantis train my staff in magnetic particle testing?
faq.a: Yes, through MT Level 1 and Level 2 training. Your company then qualifies and certifies its technicians under its own SNT-TC-1A written practice, because the employer issues that certification.

pt.title: Liquid Penetrant & Dye Penetrant Inspection | Charlotte, NC
pt.description: On-site liquid penetrant testing and dye penetrant inspection for stainless, alloy and aluminum parts at Charlotte-area plants and shops. Request a PT quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) and Dye Penetrant Inspection in Charlotte, North Carolina
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes penetrant testing technicians to Charlotte-area power plants, food and beverage plants, fabrication shops and construction sites to find surface-breaking cracks and porosity in welds and machined parts, especially in stainless steel, nickel alloys and aluminum. Request a dye penetrant quote for your Charlotte site with the material, surface condition and code, and we reply within one business day.

Where liquid penetrant testing is used in Charlotte

Penetrant testing earns its place where magnetic particle testing cannot be used. Around Charlotte that means the stainless and alloy systems in generating plants, such as feedwater heater components, chemistry lines and repair welds in high-alloy piping. It means sanitary stainless welds in the food, beverage and consumer-products plants that line the region's industrial corridors, where a surface crack is both a safety issue and a cleanability issue. It also means aluminum and stainless fabrications made for the energy equipment supply chain, and the surfaces of repair excavations that have been ground out and need to be proved crack-free before a re-weld.

  • Stainless and nickel alloy welds in power plant piping and heat exchangers
  • Sanitary stainless vessels and piping in food and beverage processing
  • Aluminum structures, housings and machined parts
  • Ground-out repair cavities and weld preparation surfaces on any alloy

Aircraft components that pass through the airport district are a different matter: aerospace fluorescent penetrant lines run to customer-specific process specifications, and Atlantis does not perform that work.

What PT finds, and what it cannot

Penetrant testing detects only discontinuities that are open to the surface. A low-viscosity liquid is drawn into a crack, pore or lap by capillary action; after the excess is removed, a developer pulls the trapped liquid back out so the indication shows as a colored or fluorescent line. The material can be ferrous or non-ferrous, magnetic or not, as long as it is non-porous.

The same principle sets the limits. A flaw that is closed at the surface, smeared over by grinding or blasting, or filled with oil, paint or scale will not take up penetrant, so cleaning and mechanical preparation matter as much as the liquid. Porous materials trap penetrant and give a heavy background. Subsurface flaws are invisible to the method. Depth cannot be measured, only the surface length and appearance.

Choosing the penetrant system

The procedure chooses among a few families. Visible dye, usually red against a white developer, is the common field choice because it needs no darkening. Fluorescent penetrant is more sensitive and is viewed under UV-A light with controlled ambient lighting. Water-washable, post-emulsifiable and solvent-removable penetrants differ in how the excess is removed, and solvent-removable systems are the usual choice for field work on welds. Developers can be dry powder, aqueous or non-aqueous wet, with non-aqueous wet developer sprayed from a can being the typical field option.

Penetrant materials for nickel-base alloys and austenitic stainless steel should be controlled for sulfur and halogen content, because residues can harm those alloys in high-temperature service. That control is stated in the procedure, and the batch information is recorded.

Technique, step by step

The surface is cleaned of oil, paint, scale and weld flux, and dried so the liquid can enter the flaw. Penetrant is applied and left to dwell for the time the procedure gives; excess is wiped away without removing penetrant from the flaw; developer is applied thinly and allowed to develop; and the surface is examined at the specified light level. ASME Section V Article 6 sets a standard temperature range of 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit for the part and the materials. Outside that range, the procedure must be qualified at the temperature in question, which matters for hot summer steel and for cold mornings in an unheated bay.

Codes and acceptance criteria for Charlotte work

The method is set by ASME Section V Article 6, and for general industry by ASTM E165, with ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8 for pressure vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.4 for process piping and B31.1 for power piping. Structural stainless work may call for AWS D1.6. Acceptance is taken from the governing code, which typically treats cracks and linear indications as rejectable and sets limits on rounded indications. Where API 510 or API 570 governs, the owner's authorized inspector is responsible for the inspection decisions and Atlantis supplies the examination records.

North Carolina and site requirements

North Carolina boilers and pressure vessels are regulated by the Boiler Safety Bureau of the state Department of Labor under the Uniform Boiler and Pressure Vessel Act. Repairs and alterations follow the National Board Inspection Code, and penetrant examination of a repair weld forms part of the paperwork. The state's own occupational safety and health plan governs chemical handling and ventilation on site; penetrant cleaners and developers are flammable and need a hazard communication review before work starts, particularly inside vessels or other confined spaces.

Removing excess penetrant, and where examinations go wrong

Most poor penetrant results come from the removal step. If too much penetrant is left on the surface, the background glows or stays pink and a real indication is hidden. If too much is removed, or solvent is sprayed directly on the surface, penetrant is washed out of the flaw and a crack is missed. Solvent-removable systems are controlled by wiping with a dry cloth first and then a cloth lightly dampened with remover, and the procedure forbids flushing. Developer should be a thin, even film; a thick white coat can mask a fine crack. These are the details a Level II technician watches, and they are the reasons the procedure specifies times and steps in order.

Penetrant sensitivity is also checked against the surface itself. A freshly machined stainless face is easy to examine, while a blasted or peened surface can close small cracks and needs etching before penetrant is applied. Weld caps with deep ripples hold developer and produce false background, so the technician may ask for light dressing. Anything done to the surface is noted on the report, since the owner's engineer should know whether a clean result was obtained on the as-welded surface or on a conditioned one.

Interpreting indications

Penetrant indications are judged when the developer has had time to work, and again after the specified final interpretation time. A crack appears as a continuous or broken line; porosity as scattered round spots; a lap or cold shut as a smooth line, often curved. Non-relevant indications come from surface roughness, scratches, bleed-out at a weld edge, or residue from earlier tests, and they are dealt with by wiping the spot, re-cleaning and re-applying developer to see whether the indication returns. Atlantis technicians record relevant indications with size and position, and acceptance depends entirely on the code, so a reject under one code may be accepted under another.

Repairs and re-examination

When a linear indication is rejected, the repair is carried out by the fabricator or contractor, and the repaired surface must be examined again after the excavation and again after the re-weld. Penetrant testing is especially useful for the excavation step, because it confirms the crack has been completely removed before welding begins. Some codes also require re-examination of the area adjacent to the repair, and the procedure should say how far to look. Keeping a clear identifier for each repair location in the report makes it possible to trace what was found, what was removed and what was accepted.

Equipment, materials and safety checks

Before work begins, the technician confirms that the penetrant, remover and developer are from the same family and compatible, that containers are in date, and that the fluorescent light meter, if used, is within calibration. A test panel with known cracks, where the procedure requires one, shows that the system is performing. Solvent cleaners and aerosol developers are flammable, so ignition sources are controlled, and in tanks or vessels ventilation and atmospheric testing come first. Waste rags and empty cans are collected for disposal under the site's hazardous waste rules. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001, and these controls are part of how the work is documented.

Who does the work

Penetrant testing is performed by Level II personnel under the company's written practice based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, with an ASNT Level III approving the procedure and reviewing records. The employer issues the qualification; training and testing support it. Atlantis holds ISO 9001 and ISO 14001 certification, and quoted scope is matched to what the written practice covers.

What the PT report contains

The report lists the component, location and drawing reference, the penetrant and developer brand, type and batch, the cleaning and removal method, dwell time and developer time, the part and material temperature, the light level, and the technician and level. Every indication is recorded with location, length and type, with a photograph where possible, and an accept or reject decision cites the code. Where a procedure demands post-cleaning after the examination, the report records that too, because residual penetrant on stainless or aluminum is itself a defect for some owners.

Planning a PT job in Charlotte

Technicians travel to your site, so conditions and cleanliness drive the plan. Humid Charlotte summers slow drying and can leave moisture in a flaw, while hot steel evaporates penetrant before it has dwelled. A shaded work area, a surface thermometer and a clear schedule of cleaning, dwell and development steps keep results repeatable. Food and beverage plants usually need documented chemical approvals and wash-down schedules before penetrant materials are allowed on product-contact surfaces. Outages at utility plants are scheduled in advance, and shop dates move with delivery calendars. We have no office in Charlotte, and the quote covers mobilization to your location.

PT, MT or UT for your Charlotte job

Use penetrant testing on stainless steel, nickel alloys, aluminum or any non-magnetic surface. On carbon steel welds, magnetic particle inspection in Charlotte is often faster and more sensitive. If the question is thickness or internal weld quality, ultrasonic testing in Charlotte is the right method. The MT versus PT comparison, the ASME explainer on Article 6 liquid penetrant requirements and the national penetrant testing page give more detail.

Training your own PT technicians

Penetrant testing is a practical entry point for new technicians. Atlantis offers PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training, and trainees can rehearse on the PT practical simulator. See the Charlotte NDT training page for local detail. Your company issues certification under its own written practice.

faq.q: What materials can liquid penetrant testing inspect?
faq.a: Any non-porous material, including stainless steel, nickel alloys, aluminum, titanium and carbon steel. It detects only discontinuities open to the surface, so it complements ultrasonic testing rather than replacing it.

faq.q: How do visible dye and fluorescent penetrant differ?
faq.a: Dye penetrant is usually red on a white developer and needs only normal light. Fluorescent penetrant glows under UV-A light and is more sensitive, but the examination area must be darkened.

faq.q: What temperature range applies to penetrant testing?
faq.a: ASME Section V Article 6 sets 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit for the part and materials. Outside that range the procedure must be qualified at the actual temperature, which matters for Charlotte summer steel.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have a team stationed in Charlotte?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Charlotte. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope, working under a written practice built on SNT-TC-1A with ASNT Level III oversight of procedures and reports.

faq.q: Does Atlantis do aerospace fluorescent penetrant work?
faq.a: No. Aircraft component penetrant lines run to customer-specific process specifications and approvals that Atlantis does not hold. Atlantis penetrant work in Charlotte is for industrial plants, fabricators and construction.

faq.q: Why does surface preparation matter so much?
faq.a: Penetrant must enter the flaw. Oil, paint, scale or smeared metal from grinding closes the opening, so a crack can go unseen. Cleaning, and sometimes etching, are part of the procedure.

faq.q: Is penetrant testing safe on stainless steel in service?
faq.a: It is when the materials are controlled for sulfur and halogens and the part is cleaned afterward. The procedure records the batch information and states whether post-cleaning is needed.

faq.q: Can penetrant testing find subsurface cracks?
faq.a: No. It only finds flaws that are open to the surface. Magnetic particle testing can sometimes find near-surface flaws in steel, and ultrasonic testing is used for internal conditions.

faq.q: What should I send to get a PT quote for Charlotte?
faq.a: Send drawings, materials, surface condition, the governing code and edition, the system type you prefer if any, access conditions, and dates. Mention any chemical approvals your site requires.

rt.title: Radiography Alternatives & Level III Support | Charlotte, NC
rt.description: Atlantis does not perform radiography in the US. For Charlotte, NC we offer UT where codes allow, plus ASNT Level III review of radiographs and images.
rt.h1: Radiographic Testing (RT) Alternatives in Charlotte, North Carolina
rt.html:
On projects in the United States, Atlantis does not perform radiographic testing of any kind. Industrial radiography is a licensed activity, governed by Nuclear Regulatory Commission rules in 10 CFR Part 34 or the equivalent rules of an Agreement State, and it is not a service Atlantis offers here. If you searched for RT in Charlotte, this page explains what Atlantis does provide for the same inspection need.

Why radiography is licensed, and how North Carolina fits

Radiography uses a sealed gamma source or an X-ray tube, and the people and companies that expose film or detectors must hold a radioactive materials or radiation machine registration for the jurisdiction. North Carolina is an NRC Agreement State, so a contractor working in Charlotte is regulated under the state's radiation protection program rather than directly by the NRC. Radiographers also work inside controlled boundaries, and a plant must clear or shut down adjacent work areas. Atlantis does not take on that work, and does not recommend or refer to a particular radiography contractor.

Ultrasonic testing as a volumetric alternative

Where the construction code and the owner allow it, ultrasonic examination can serve as the volumetric method for welds. ASME B31.3 and API 1104 contain provisions for ultrasonic examination of production welds, AWS D1.1 has its own ultrasonic acceptance criteria for groove welds, and ASME Section VIII permits ultrasonic examination in place of radiography only under specific conditions. None of these substitutions is automatic. The owner, the design engineer and, for code work, the authorized inspector must agree on the method before the job, and the agreement should be written into the procedure and the quality plan. Where that agreement exists, Atlantis technicians travel to your site for ultrasonic weld inspection in Charlotte, with the scan plan, reference level and acceptance criteria stated up front. A radiation boundary is not needed, so other trades can keep working nearby.

ASNT Level III radiography support that needs no radiation license

Reading and judging radiographs does not require a radiation license, because no source is handled. Atlantis can support Charlotte-area owners with an ASNT Level III who reviews radiographs, whether film or digital images, together with technique sheets, against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code. Typical requests are a second read on disputed indications, a check that image quality indicators and density met the technique, and a review of an RT contractor's procedure and written practice. Anoop Rayavarapu holds ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. These reviews are done on documents and images sent to us, and they help owners accept or reject work from an RT contractor with confidence. See ASNT Level III consulting and written practice development for how these engagements are set up.

RT training theory

Technicians who want to understand radiographic interpretation can study the theory through the radiographic testing Level 2 course. Hands-on source handling and the practical examination belong to a licensed employer, and certification is issued by the employer under its own written practice based on SNT-TC-1A.

Other methods Atlantis provides in Charlotte

For surface cracking, the options are magnetic particle inspection in Charlotte on carbon and low-alloy steel and liquid penetrant testing in Charlotte on stainless steel and non-magnetic alloys. All field work is carried out by technicians mobilized to your site, since Atlantis has no office in Charlotte. Request a quote for ultrasonic work in Charlotte with your drawings and the code your weld must meet.

faq.q: Is radiography available from Atlantis in Charlotte?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not carry out radiography anywhere in the United States, because industrial radiography is licensed under NRC rules or the equivalent Agreement State rules. Atlantis offers other methods and Level III review instead.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing replace radiography on my welds?
faq.a: Only where your construction code and owner allow it. ASME B31.3, API 1104, AWS D1.1 and ASME Section VIII each treat ultrasonic examination differently, so agree the substitution with the engineer and inspector first.

faq.q: Can Atlantis review radiographs taken by another contractor?
faq.a: Yes. An ASNT Level III can review film or digital images and technique sheets against ASME Section V Article 2 and the code, and give a second read on disputed indications. No radiation license is needed for review.

faq.q: Where can I study radiographic testing theory?
faq.a: A radiographic testing Level 2 course from Atlantis covers the theory. Source handling and the practical examination are done by a licensed employer, which then certifies its own staff under SNT-TC-1A.

faq.q: Does Atlantis recommend radiography contractors in Charlotte?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not name or recommend radiography contractors. We can review the contractor procedure and images you already have, or provide ultrasonic, magnetic particle and penetrant work.
